title: A shared vocabulary for agent design
lead: A systematic review of 57 studies distilled 18 architectural patterns for foundation-model agents.
cues: Inside the agent: goal creation, planning, reflection.
Outside it: the model, knowledge, a registry, tools and workers.
Each pattern documents context, forces, solution, consequences, known uses.
Why it matters: two teams can compare designs precisely.
takeaway: Patterns let us name a design choice and its trade-off.
source: Liu et al. (2025), Agent Design Pattern Catalogue, JSS 220, §2–4, Fig. 2

title: Eighteen patterns in eight families
lead: Group the catalogue by the question each pattern answers.
cues: Eight families, from goal creation to evaluation.
Most agents combine several small patterns.
Deep dive on three: planning, reflection, registry.
Coding harnesses skip RAG and use grep and the language server instead.
takeaway: Most agents combine many small patterns, not one big one.
source: Liu et al. (2025), Agent Design Pattern Catalogue, JSS 220, Table 1 · Barbaste et al. (2026), Harness Engineering, arXiv:2609.00006, §13.2

title: Planning: one path or many?
lead: A plan generator decomposes a goal; the choice is how many options it keeps open.
cues: Single path: one ordered list — cheap, simple, explainable.
Multi-path: options per step, compared before choosing.
Trade-off: multi-path improves certainty but costs more model calls.
A visible plan lets people correct it early.
takeaway: Most coding agents choose a single, visible plan.
source: Liu et al. (2025), Agent Design Pattern Catalogue, JSS 220, §4.7–4.8

title: Reflection: who checks the work?
lead: Reflection patterns differ by who gives the feedback: the agent, another agent, or a person.
cues: Self: cheap and fast, limited by the agent’s own blind spots.
Cross: a second agent adds a perspective, and cost.
Human: aligns with preferences, adds latency and contestability.
Real harnesses mix all three at different moments.
takeaway: Choose the reviewer by the cost of a wrong action.
source: Liu et al. (2025), Agent Design Pattern Catalogue, JSS 220, §4.9–4.11 · Barbaste et al. (2026), Harness Engineering, arXiv:2609.00006, §6

title: Registries and adapters: finding capabilities
lead: A registry makes tools and agents discoverable; an adapter connects the loop to outside systems.
cues: Registry: tool schemas, skills and agent personas in one place.
Load on use: skills and agents enter the context only when needed.
Adapter: MCP or JSON-RPC to servers, language servers and sandboxes.
Scale: Hermes registers 69 tools but shows each platform a subset.
takeaway: Registries keep the loop small while capabilities grow.
source: Liu et al. (2025), Agent Design Pattern Catalogue, JSS 220, §4.16–4.17 · Barbaste et al. (2026), Harness Engineering, arXiv:2609.00006, §8

title: Choosing patterns: the decision model
lead: The catalogue’s decision model asks one question per design problem.
cues: One question per row, two answers.
Each answer has consequences — benefits and costs.
A design is a coherent set of answers.
Next: how do we judge whether the choices are good?
takeaway: A pattern is chosen by a question, not by fashion.
source: Liu et al. (2025), Agent Design Pattern Catalogue, JSS 220, §5.1, Fig. 19
